units.title: Emergence of Psychology
units.description: Build the story of psychology as a discipline: where its questions came from, how Indian and Western intellectual traditions shaped them, and how major schools and paradigms changed the subject. Move from philosophical roots to the emergence of scientific psychology, then compare the assumptions, methods, and objects of study that distinguish major traditions. By the end of the unit, you should be able to place major thinkers and schools in context and explain why psychology developed in different directions.

units.title: Research Methodology and Statistics
units.description: Build a complete research-to-evidence framework for psychology. Start with how research questions become variables, hypotheses, samples, designs, and ethical decisions, then connect these choices to measurement, data collection, and interpretation. In the statistics portion, develop the reasoning behind probability, distributions, statistical tests, power, effect size, correlation, regression, and factor analysis so that you can identify which method fits a research question and interpret what the result actually means.

topics.title: Research: Meaning, Purpose and Dimensions
topics.explanation: Research is systematic, controlled, empirical and critical inquiry. In psychology, research questions are translated into observable evidence so explanations can be tested rather than accepted from intuition alone. Distinguish exploratory/formulative work, which develops insight, from hypothesis-testing work, which evaluates specified propositions.
topics.notes:
CORE IDEA
Research is a disciplined way to answer a question using evidence. Kerlinger's definition in the supplied NET preparation text emphasizes systematic, controlled, empirical and critical investigation of hypothetical propositions about presumed relations among phenomena.

PURPOSES
• Exploratory/formulative research: develop familiarity, clarify a problem and generate new insights or hypotheses.
• Hypothesis-testing research: collect evidence to evaluate a specified prediction or relationship.
• Psychology's broad scientific goals include describing, explaining, predicting and (where justified) influencing behaviour.

RESEARCH LOGIC
Question → literature/context → operationally answerable problem → evidence plan → data → analysis → conclusion → report/replication.

EXAM DISTINCTION
A research question identifies what needs explaining; a hypothesis is a testable proposed answer. Data may support or fail to support a hypothesis; a result is not proof merely because it fits an expectation.

SOURCE BASIS
The uploaded PowerWithin NET Psychology material defines scientific research and distinguishes exploratory/formulative from hypothesis-testing research. Ciccarelli and White's Psychology (6th ed.) describes the scientific approach as question, hypothesis, testing/data analysis, conclusion and reporting.

topics.title: Research Problems, Variables, Hypotheses and Sampling
topics.explanation: A well-defined problem determines the evidence needed and shapes variables, operational definitions, hypotheses, sampling and design. Variables vary across people, settings or time; operational definitions specify how a construct is observed, manipulated or scored.
topics.notes:
RESEARCH-PROBLEM SEQUENCE
Problem/question → identify constructs and variables → define how each variable will be measured or manipulated → state a testable hypothesis → select population/sample and method.

VARIABLES
• Independent variable (IV): the factor manipulated or treated as a predictor in an experiment.
• Dependent variable (DV): the outcome measured to evaluate the effect or association.
• Extraneous variable: another factor that may influence the outcome.
• Confound: an alternative factor systematically entangled with the condition/predictor, making interpretation difficult.

OPERATIONAL DEFINITION
A concrete statement of the procedure used to measure or manipulate a variable. Example: “test performance” might be operationalized as the number of correct answers on a specified test; this is an example, not a universal definition.

HYPOTHESES
• Null hypothesis (H₀): typically states no effect or no relationship in the population under the specified model.
• Alternative hypothesis (H₁/Ha): states the effect or relationship being investigated.
• A directional hypothesis predicts the direction; a non-directional hypothesis predicts a difference/relationship without specifying direction.

ERRORS
Type I error: reject a true null hypothesis (false positive).
Type II error: fail to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative).
Do not confuse these with whether the study's substantive idea is important.

SAMPLING
Population is the target group; sample is the subset actually studied. Sampling bias occurs when the selection process systematically misrepresents the target population. Random selection and random assignment are different: selection concerns who enters the sample; assignment concerns which condition participants enter.

SOURCE BASIS
The uploaded PowerWithin NET material explicitly lists research problems, variables, operational definitions, hypotheses and sampling, and distinguishes IV/DV. Psychology—A Self-Teaching Guide explains Type I/II errors and experimental variables.

topics.title: Research Ethics
topics.explanation: Ethics applies to participant recruitment, consent, risk, privacy, data handling, analysis, authorship and reporting. Protecting participants and reporting evidence honestly are parts of sound research, not optional additions.
topics.notes:
PARTICIPANT PROTECTION
• Seek voluntary, informed consent when required; explain the study in understandable language and relevant risks/limits.
• Minimize physical, psychological, social and privacy risks.
• Respect the right to withdraw, subject to clearly explained practical/legal limits.
• Protect confidentiality and store identifiable data securely.
• Use deception only where ethically justified and approved, and debrief participants when appropriate.
• Research with children or other groups requiring additional safeguards needs appropriate permission and protections.

RESEARCH INTEGRITY
Do not fabricate data, falsify records, plagiarize, selectively misrepresent findings or claim certainty beyond the evidence. Report methods and limitations sufficiently for scrutiny and replication. Authorship should reflect actual scholarly contribution.

REVIEW
Ciccarelli and White describe institutional review boards/ethics review as a safeguard that examines proposed studies for participant safety and ethical treatment. Ethical approval does not remove the researcher's responsibility during the study.

EXAM CUE
Separate ethics in conducting research (consent, harm, privacy, review) from ethics in reporting research (honesty, attribution, accurate representation and responsible authorship).

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli and White, Psychology (6th ed.), section on guidelines for research with people, discusses avoiding physical/psychological harm and institutional review.

topics.title: Research Paradigms
topics.explanation: Research paradigms differ in assumptions about knowledge and reality, the questions they prioritize, and how they treat evidence. Quantitative and qualitative approaches are not merely numerical versus verbal data; they often differ in research logic and interpretation. Mixed methods intentionally integrates both.
topics.notes:
QUANTITATIVE APPROACH
Typically uses structured measurement and numerical data to describe patterns, test hypotheses, estimate relationships or compare groups. Quality depends on suitable measurement, design, sampling and analysis—not numbers alone.

QUALITATIVE APPROACH
Investigates meaning, experience, context and process using approaches such as interviews, observation, narratives or textual material. Interpretation and reflexivity matter; findings should be judged against the question and evidence rather than treated as automatically generalizable.

MIXED METHODS
Combines quantitative and qualitative evidence within one inquiry. Strong mixed-methods work explains why both are needed and how findings are integrated; simply collecting two kinds of data is not sufficient integration.

PARADIGM NOTE
The uploaded PowerWithin text contrasts logical positivist assumptions (including realism, objectivist epistemology and experimental/manipulative methodology) with critical perspectives that treat knowledge as value-mediated and reality as shaped by social, political, cultural and economic forces. Preserve the distinction as presented in that source; paradigm labels can be used differently across authors.

EXAM STRATEGY
Compare the approach by: research question, assumptions, data, sampling, analysis, researcher role and claim that the evidence can support.

SOURCE BASIS
The uploaded PowerWithin material lists quantitative, qualitative and mixed-methods approaches and discusses logical positivism, post-positivism and critical perspectives.

topics.title: Methods of Research
topics.explanation: Choose a method according to the question, feasibility, ethics and the kind of inference required. Describing a pattern, understanding an experience, estimating association and testing a causal effect require different designs.
topics.notes:
METHOD-MATCHING GUIDE
• Naturalistic observation: observe behaviour in its ordinary setting; strong for context, limited control over causes.
• Laboratory observation: observe in a structured setting; greater control may reduce naturalness.
• Survey: gather self-reports from a sample using interviews or questionnaires; wording, memory and social-desirability effects can bias responses.
• Interview: flexible probing can add depth; interviewer effects and analysis demands matter.
• Questionnaire: efficient standardized responses; item clarity, response options and nonresponse matter.
• Case study: intensive study of a person, group or case; rich detail but limited basis for broad generalization.
• Experiment: manipulate an IV, measure a DV and control alternatives; random assignment strengthens causal inference.
• Quasi-experiment: evaluates an intervention/exposure without full random assignment; selection and history may threaten causal conclusions.
• Field study: studies behaviour in real-world contexts.
• Cross-cultural study: compares cultural groups or contexts; consider equivalence of measures and avoid treating cultural groups as internally uniform.
• Phenomenology: explores lived experience and its meaning.
• Grounded theory: develops an explanatory account/theory through iterative data collection and analysis.
• Focus group: facilitated group discussion; interaction is data, but dominant voices and confidentiality are concerns.
• Narrative research: studies stories and how people organize experience.
• Ethnography: sustained study of a culture-sharing group, practices and context.

CORRELATION WARNING
Correlation estimates direction/strength of association; it does not by itself establish that one variable causes another.

EXAM STRATEGY
For each method learn purpose, data source, procedure, strengths, limitations and the strongest inference it can justify.

SOURCE BASIS
Ciccarelli and White's Psychology (6th ed.) summarizes naturalistic/laboratory observation, case studies and surveys, and identifies experimentation as the method that permits causal conclusions through manipulation and control. The uploaded NET material lists the methods above.

topics.title: Statistics in Psychology
topics.explanation: Descriptive statistics summarize a dataset. Measures of central tendency describe its typical location; measures of dispersion describe variability. Match the statistic to the distribution and measurement context.
topics.notes:
CENTRAL TENDENCY
• Mean: arithmetic average; sensitive to extreme scores.
• Median: middle score after ordering; more resistant to extreme values.
• Mode: most frequent value/category; useful for categorical data and distributions with repeated peaks.

DISPERSION
• Range: maximum minus minimum; depends only on extremes.
• Variance: average squared deviation under the relevant population/sample convention.
• Standard deviation: square root of variance, expressed in the original score units.

INTERPRETATION
A mean alone can hide spread or skew. Two groups may have the same mean but different variability. Inspect the distribution and outliers before choosing or interpreting a summary.

SOURCE BASIS
The uploaded NET material includes measures of central tendency and dispersion. This note supplies the standard conceptual distinctions needed to organize that listed syllabus content.

topics.title: Normal Probability Curve
topics.explanation: The normal probability curve is a symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution in which mean, median and mode coincide. Standard-deviation units help interpret relative standing when the normal model is appropriate.
topics.notes:
KEY PROPERTIES
• Symmetric and unimodal; mean = median = mode at the centre.
• Total area under the curve equals 1 (100% probability).
• Tails approach but do not meet the horizontal axis.
• A z score expresses distance from the mean in standard-deviation units: z = (score − mean) / SD.

EMPIRICAL RULE
For an approximately normal distribution, about 68% of observations lie within ±1 SD, about 95% within ±2 SD and about 99.7% within ±3 SD.

CAUTION
The empirical rule applies to a normal distribution or a close approximation, not automatically to every dataset. A z score's interpretation depends on the reference distribution and the correctness of the mean/SD used.

SOURCE BASIS

topics.title: Parametric and Non-Parametric Tests
topics.explanation: Select a test using the outcome scale, independence or pairing of observations, number of groups, distributional assumptions and the hypothesis. Parametric and non-parametric tests are not interchangeable labels for “strong” and “weak” tests.
topics.notes:
PARAMETRIC TESTS
Use model-based assumptions about population parameters/distributions. The t-test commonly compares means in one-sample, independent-groups or paired designs, subject to the relevant assumptions.

NON-PARAMETRIC TESTS
Often use ranks or signs and can be suitable when assumptions for a particular parametric procedure are not met or the data structure is ordinal. They still have assumptions and are not automatically assumption-free.

COMMON MATCHES
• Sign test: direction of paired differences/median-related question.
• Wilcoxon signed-rank: paired or one-sample rank-based alternative using difference ranks.
• Mann–Whitney U: two independent groups, rank-based comparison.
• Kruskal–Wallis: three or more independent groups, rank-based comparison.
• Friedman test: three or more related/repeated conditions, rank-based comparison.
• t-test: mean comparison for one or two groups depending on design.

DECISION CHECK
First identify whether observations are independent or related; then number of groups, outcome scale, target parameter and assumptions. Never choose solely by memorizing a test name.

SOURCE BASIS

topics.title: Power Analysis
topics.explanation: Statistical power is the probability of rejecting a false null hypothesis under a specified effect and model. It is related to sample size, effect size, significance level, design and measurement quality.
topics.notes:
CORE RELATIONSHIPS
Power = 1 − β, where β is the probability of a Type II error under the specified alternative.
Power generally increases with larger sample size, larger true effect, less measurement noise and a higher alpha threshold, all else equal.

PLANNING
A power analysis can inform the sample size needed to detect a prespecified effect with a target probability. It should be based on a defensible effect-size assumption and the planned analysis/design.

CAUTION
A non-significant result does not prove that no effect exists; the study may have low power or imprecise measurement. A statistically significant result does not by itself show that an effect is practically important.

topics.title: Effect Size
topics.explanation: Effect size describes the magnitude of a difference or relationship. It complements significance testing, which also depends on sample size and variability.
topics.notes:
INTERPRETATION
A p-value addresses compatibility of data with a statistical model/null hypothesis; effect size addresses how large the observed or estimated effect is on a chosen scale.

COMMON FORMS
Depending on the analysis, effect size may be expressed as a standardized mean difference, correlation, proportion of variance explained or another design-appropriate index.

REPORTING
Interpret effect size in the research context, with uncertainty where possible. Avoid treating universal small/medium/large cut-offs as substitutes for substantive judgment.

topics.title: Correlational Analysis
topics.explanation: Correlation describes the direction and strength of association between variables. Product-moment and rank-order methods answer related but not identical questions; partial and multiple correlation extend the number of variables considered.
topics.notes:
PEARSON PRODUCT-MOMENT
Pearson's r describes the strength and direction of a linear association between quantitative variables. It ranges from −1 to +1. A value near zero indicates little linear association, not necessarily no relationship of any form.

SPEARMAN RANK-ORDER
Spearman's rho works with ranks and assesses monotonic association; it is useful when rank information is meaningful or Pearson's linearity assumptions are unsuitable.

PARTIAL CORRELATION
Examines association between two variables while statistically controlling one or more other variables.

MULTIPLE CORRELATION
Represents the relationship between one criterion and a set of predictors, often summarized by R.

CAUSALITY
Association alone does not establish cause. Directionality, third variables, selection and measurement can explain an observed correlation.

SOURCE BASIS

topics.title: Special Correlation Methods
topics.explanation: Special correlation coefficients are chosen according to how variables are measured and categorized. Learn the measurement structure behind each coefficient rather than memorizing names in isolation.
topics.notes:
COMMON COEFFICIENTS
• Point-biserial: association between a continuous variable and a genuinely dichotomous variable.
• Biserial: association between a continuous variable and an artificially dichotomized underlying continuous variable, under additional assumptions.
• Phi coefficient: association between two dichotomous variables in a 2 × 2 table.
• Tetrachoric: estimates association between two underlying continuous variables that have both been dichotomized, under a latent-distribution model.

MEMORY CUE
Ask what each variable represents before choosing the coefficient: continuous + true dichotomy (point-biserial); continuous + artificial dichotomy (biserial); two true dichotomies (phi); two underlying continuous variables dichotomized (tetrachoric).

CAUTION
The assumptions behind biserial and tetrachoric coefficients matter; they should not be applied to every binary variable automatically.

SOURCE BASIS
The uploaded NET Psychology Unit 2 syllabus lists biserial, point-biserial, tetrachoric and phi coefficients. The variable-structure distinctions are standard statistical definitions used to clarify the list.

topics.title: Regression
topics.explanation: Regression models an outcome in relation to one or more predictors. It is used for prediction and estimation; causal interpretation requires an appropriate design and defensible assumptions, not merely a regression equation.
topics.notes:
SIMPLE LINEAR REGRESSION
Models an outcome from one predictor, commonly written Ŷ = a + bX. The slope b represents the expected change in predicted Y for a one-unit increase in X within the model.

MULTIPLE REGRESSION
Uses several predictors to estimate the outcome. Each coefficient describes the predictor's association with the outcome holding the other included predictors constant, under the model.

INTERPRETATION
Distinguish prediction from explanation and association from causation. Check linearity, residual patterns, influential observations, multicollinearity and the suitability of the model for the data.

SOURCE BASIS

topics.title: Factor Analysis
topics.explanation: Factor analysis investigates patterns of covariation among observed variables to represent them with a smaller number of underlying dimensions. Interpretability depends on appropriate data, extraction choices, rotation and theory-informed judgment.
topics.notes:
PURPOSE
Factor analysis seeks to summarize shared patterns among observed variables through a smaller set of latent factors. It is not simply a procedure for naming clusters without examining evidence.

WORKFLOW
1. Check whether the data and correlation structure are suitable.
2. Choose an extraction approach appropriate to the goal and assumptions.
3. Decide how many factors to retain using multiple sources of evidence.
4. Rotate factors where appropriate to aid interpretation.
5. Examine loadings, cross-loadings, communalities and conceptual coherence.
6. Label factors cautiously and report decisions transparently.

ROTATION
Orthogonal rotation constrains factors to be uncorrelated; oblique rotation allows factors to correlate. Choice should follow theoretical and empirical considerations, not a blanket rule.

CAUTION
A factor label is an interpretation, not a directly observed fact. Different analytic choices can yield different solutions.

topics.title: Experimental Designs
topics.explanation: Experimental designs organize manipulation, comparison, control and measurement. Match a design to the research question and whether participants are assigned to independent groups, measured repeatedly or organized into blocks/time points.
topics.notes:
DESIGN LOGIC
A design specifies how conditions, participants and observations are arranged to address a question while reducing alternative explanations.

KEY DESIGNS
• Randomized block design: groups/blocks participants or units by a relevant source of variation, then randomizes conditions within blocks.
• Repeated-measures design: the same participants contribute observations across conditions or times; consider order, practice, fatigue and carryover effects.
• Latin square: balances the positions/order of multiple conditions across rows and columns under its design constraints.
• Cohort study: follows a defined group across time or compares outcomes by exposure/cohort; often observational.
• Time-series design: repeated observations before and/or after an event or intervention.
• Single-subject design: repeated measurement of an individual/case across baseline and intervention phases.
• MANOVA: multivariate analysis of variance for multiple related dependent variables.
• ANCOVA: analysis of covariance, combining group comparison with covariate adjustment under model assumptions.

DISTINCTION
Random assignment can strengthen causal inference; repeated observation alone does not make a study experimental. Cohort and time-series labels describe different structures and do not guarantee control of confounds.

SOURCE BASIS

topics.title: ANOVA
topics.explanation: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) evaluates mean differences across groups/conditions by comparing between-group variation with within-group variation. Factorial ANOVA also examines interactions between factors.
topics.notes:
ONE-WAY ANOVA
Tests whether there is evidence that not all group means are equal for one categorical factor. A significant omnibus result does not by itself identify which groups differ; follow-up comparisons may be needed.

FACTORIAL ANOVA
Examines two or more factors and can estimate main effects and interactions.

MAIN EFFECT
The effect of one factor averaged over the levels of the other factor(s), according to the model.

INTERACTION
The effect of one factor changes depending on the level of another factor. Inspect the pattern of means/estimated effects rather than interpreting main effects in isolation when an interaction is important.

POST-HOC COMPARISONS
Used to investigate which comparisons account for a broader group difference, with an appropriate method for controlling error across comparisons.
